title: Staggered fintech adoption on loan default rates

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
We will use a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach to estimate the causal effect of fintech adoption on loan default rates. The DID method is appropriate here because we have a treatment group (banks that adopted fintech) and a control group (banks that did not adopt fintech), and we can observe their loan default rates before and after the treatment. The key assumption for DID is that the treatment and control groups would have followed the same trend in loan default rates in the absence of the treatment.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(plm)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s08_data.csv")

# Convert the data to a panel data frame
pdata <- pdata.frame(data, index = c("unit_id", "period"))

# Run the DID regression
did_model <- plm(y ~ treat_x_post, data = pdata, model = "within")

# Print the coefficient for the treatment effect
coeftest(did_model, vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1"))

# Robustness check: cluster-robust standard errors
coeftest(did_model, vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1", cluster = pdata$unit_id))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
We expect the coefficient on the `treat_x_post` variable to be negative, indicating that the adoption of fintech reduced loan default rates. The magnitude of the effect will depend on the data, but we expect a substantial reduction given the potential for algorithmic credit scoring to improve risk assessment and lending decisions. The robustness check using cluster-robust standard errors will help account for potential within-unit correlation in the error terms, which could affect the validity of the standard errors in the main regression.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Staggered DID (Callaway-Sant'Anna or Sun-Abraham) — cohort-specific ATTs; treatment=fintech adoption
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Fintech-adopting banks reduce default rates relative to non-adopters
